@DamonZwicker @Jimmyshi — 8309 needs five edits and you're both on the author line, so flagging
before I touch the PR rather than after.

What happened. Obaresearch posted a careful review on the thread on 24 Sept (#30), I answered
the same day (#31), and he endorsed the answers (#32). That was mid-outage on my side, so if it went
past you, that's why. He finished with "looking forward to the diff" and I finished with "I'll post
the diff here once these land". Nothing has landed — #1826 hasn't been touched since 21 August.

The two substantive ones (he called them "the two clearest underspecifications"):

1. Cursor ordering. The cursor is opaque and the spec never says what it orders by, or which clock
   since filters on. If a node orders by origin timestamp, a record relayed after a partition
   arrives with an older timestamp, lands *behind* a peer's cursor, and is never pulled — silent
   record loss after any partition. Fix: cursor MUST advance in local ingestion order, and since
   is defined against that same clock.
2. Future-dated records. No bound today. Fix: a node MUST reject records whose timestamp exceeds
   local time by more than a bounded tolerance.

Three smaller ones: a SHOULD to deprioritise peers that repeatedly serve records failing
signature verification; a SHOULD that namespaces be rooted in an ENS name the operator controls
(example.eth:agent-attestations) — Obaresearch explicitly backed this; and moving the concrete
namespace examples out of the normative Namespaces section into Reference Implementation so the
normative text stays transport-only.

Damon — what is NOT changing, since your companion composes against it. The divergence rule is
untouched: two validly-signed records with the same (inputHash, namespace) and a differing value
remain a divergence, not a duplicate, both MUST be retained, and resolveDivergence stays exposed
without the base prescribing what resolves it. That boundary is exactly where we left it in #29 and
I'm not moving it.

One thing that is genuinely a joint call. That fifth edit moves the agent-attestations:wyriwe
reference out of normative text. It stays in the document, in Reference Implementation — but WYRIWE is
8299 and that has five of us on it, so say if you'd rather it stayed normative. My read is that
8309 reads stronger as transport-only and stack-agnostic, which is also Obaresearch's point.

And a housekeeping question while the file is open: two section headers carry working annotations
— ### Namespaces — *(LOCKED: no on-chain registry; out-of-band convention)* and the same on Protocol
versioning — with no legend in the document. They make sense to us as settled-decision notes, but an
editor reviewing this will likely read them as stray non-spec text. I'd fold them into Rationale
lines in the same pass unless either of you wants them kept as-is.

I'll hold off pushing for a day in case there are objections. After it lands I'll post the diff on the
thread, which is what he's waiting on.

On the fifth edit -- no objection from the 8299 side. 8309 already says it doesn't interpret namespace contents, so moving the wyriwe mention into Reference Implementation is reorganizing an example, not cutting a real coupling. Final call on normative vs. not is yours and Damon's as the base-8309 authors.

We’ve validated the issues we discussed yesterday. However, the OP-level abstraction and autotune logic haven’t been implemented yet, so we’ll need a bit more time before I can get back to you with the full update.

We’re excited to start benchmarking once this work is finished. One practical note: the current CPU version already runs pretty fast. We haven’t yet fully explored which computations can be offloaded to the GPU, so there’s still untapped potential there.

@Jimmyshi that’s a serious result — 19.6 min to ~32s end-to-end is not a tuning win, it’s a different
regime. And the shape of it is the interesting part: 9× from row-parallel matmul and 1.8× from the
parallel sumcheck means the remaining time is real work rather than overhead, which is the healthy
place to be before an autotuner goes near it.

All three of my questions are answered, and two of them dissolved rather than resolved — thank
you. Taking them in turn so nothing is assumed:

GPU arch. You said sm_89 → sm_80 can be adapted later and isn’t blocking. Agreed, and the
CPU numbers make it clearly second-order now. Happy to do that port myself when it matters, so it
doesn’t sit on your list.
Sharding granularity. This is the one that stopped being a question. I had it down as a
decision to make before we started, because 256 GB/node seemed like it might force the shard shape.
If granularity is what the autotuner searches on the hardware, there is nothing to decide in
advance — Deucalion just becomes the substrate it searches over.
OP abstraction + autotune pipeline. Understood that these need more time, and nothing on our
side is blocked by waiting.
What that changes for the allocation, with numbers. At your measured figures — 32s wall, 64
threads — one GPT-2 512 proof costs about 0.57 core-hours. Against 50,000 CPU core-hours:

regime core-h per proof proofs inside the budget
op-granularity (19.6 min) 20.9 ~2,400
layer-granularity (5.5 min) 5.9 ~8,500
layer-parallel (now) 0.57 ~88,000
Even halving that for parallel efficiency on unfamiliar hardware leaves ~44,000 runs. So the
allocation has stopped being a proving budget and become a search budget — which is exactly what
granularity × backend × layout wants. Your 3.5× and then the jump to ~32s moved it by roughly 35×.

Three Deucalion specifics worth knowing before the autotuner meets it, because they shape what a
sweep can look like rather than whether it runs:

Job arrays are the native shape. --array=1-N%K with a concurrency cap, large-x86 giving up
to 128 nodes × 128 cores and a 72h wall. A granularity sweep is a natural array; one long job is
the wrong fit.
A node is 128 cores / 256 GB — twice the threads of your bench box, so the first useful
measurement is simply how the layer-parallel path scales 64 → 128. That one number recalibrates
every estimate above, and it needs nothing from you.
GPU compute nodes have no outbound network (only login and dev-x86/dev-arm). Weights and
crates get pre-fetched on a login node and jobs run offline. Worth knowing early because it is the
kind of thing that fails after you have queued and waited rather than at submit time.
On Gemma 3 and larger models — agreed, and that is the right ambition for this window. One honest
caveat from our side: the grant is training and research only, never serving (“nunca em
produção”), so benchmark and autotune runs are squarely in scope and anything that looks like a
hosted prover is not.

I’ll do the 64 → 128 scaling run as soon as the account is live and bring you the number, since it
costs you nothing and makes the autotune search space concrete.

text_original: 32s end-to-end is a real jump, congrats -- went through the nested-parallelism note in benchmarks.md/spec.md (22.6s vs the ~6s theoretical). Checked bench_gpt2_512_full.rs on main (e10df3f): the outer 12-layer loop is still std::thread::scope (line 61), not rayon::par_iter -- so if that switch landed, it's not in the harness I'm seeing. If it hasn't: calling into the same global rayon pool from 12 independent OS threads means every inner par_iter (sumcheck.rs:382/409, ops.rs:126) goes through rayon's foreign-thread join path 12x concurrently instead of nesting natively -- making the OUTER loop itself a rayon par_iter so outer+inner share one work-stealing domain is the standard fix for that shape. But worth measuring both before assuming that's it: 12 full d=1024/ffn=4096 witness+proof buffers in flight at once could just be memory-bandwidth bound, in which case per-task pool partitioning (ThreadPoolBuilder per outer slot, not shared global) is the one that actually helps, not nesting. Happy to try both against bench_gpt2_512_full.rs and report real numbers if that's useful to you.

One more pass before the five edits land — two interactions look worth making explicit.
On cursor/since: local ingestion order fixes the late-relay loss, agreed. But since=<unix> needs a named server-local ingestion timestamp if it is to use the same ordering domain; ingestion order itself is not a clock. I’d define ingested_at as node-local metadata (not part of the signed record), with cursor advancing over that ingestion order. Also, if cursor is combined with since/namespace, the continuation token should be bound to the same filter set; otherwise an opaque cursor obtained under one query can be replayed under another and pagination semantics are under-specified.
On the ENS-rooting SHOULD: be careful with “an ENS name the operator controls.” Divergence identity is (inputHash, namespace). If each transport operator roots the same logical namespace under its own ENS name, e.g. alice.eth:agent-attestations vs bob.eth:agent-attestations, those records can no longer meet in the same divergence set at all. If the intended root is the owner/authority of the semantic namespace rather than the mesh node serving it, I’d say that explicitly.
One smaller point: “future-dated by more than a bounded tolerance” needs either a concrete maximum skew or a normative bound on the configurable tolerance. Otherwise any finite value, including an effectively unlimited one, satisfies the sentence.
None of these touch the resolveDivergence companion; they’re transport semantics.

Checked all three against erc-8309-vantage's pinned schema + golden_sets (same check as the cursor/since one): zero references to namespace, cursor/since, or a skew bound anywhere in our companion's conformance surface, so none of this forces a change there either -- all transport semantics, as you said.

On substance, for what it's worth: the ingested_at-as-node-local-metadata framing is the right shape -- keeps the signed record itself clock-independent and makes cursor/since advance over something a single node actually controls, rather than trusting origin timestamps it can't verify. Worth being explicit in the base spec about whether ENS-rooting names the semantic-namespace owner or the serving node -- those are different design points with different failure modes, and only one of them stays compatible with how divergence identity is actually computed downstream.

Gemma 3 270M is proved end-to-end — went smoother than expected.

1154 ops (18 layers: GQA 4×256 head_dim / 1 KV head, QK RMSNorm, RoPE, post-norm sandwich, gated-GELU MLP), per-layer sharding (22 shards):

- seq=16: prove 30.4s + verify 15.8s ≈ 46.2s total, ~28 GB RSS, argmax 16/16
- seq=512: prove 52.5s + verify 37.9s ≈ 90.4s total, ~39 GB RSS, argmax 469/512

The only genuinely new primitive was RoPE (rotate-half convention, two virtual sumchecks) — everything else reused the existing ops, the gated-GELU MLP is just Projection + GeluIndex + ScaleVec, no new op. Two gotchas worth pinning for anyone touching Gemma-family models: the RMSNorm weights use the "1 + gamma" convention (not the raw weight), and the residual stream grows enough that the rsqrt lookup needed a wider coarse range.

The seq=512 drop to 91.6% argmax I read as Q16 fidelity at scale, not soundness: seq=16 is 100%, the first 16 positions of seq=512 match seq=16 exactly, and verify passes throughout. Precision pass is a follow-up, not a blocker.

Next I'd like to take the DeepSeek MoE route (V2-Lite first: 15.7B total / 2.4B active, MLA + top-6 experts). Rough estimate: the MoE sparsity is actually in our favor here — commit all experts once but only load/open the routed ones, so per-proof cost tracks the activated subset rather than the total. If that holds, the big-parameter jump (V4.1-Flash 552B) becomes mostly a memory/lazy-opening problem rather than a proving blowup.

Gemma3 end-to-end at 46-90s with only RoPE as new primitive is a real result -- 18 layers, GQA+QK-norm+RoPE+gated-GELU reusing everything else is good evidence the op interface is actually stable, not just working for GPT2/TimesFM by coincidence.

Went through RoPE + verify_shard_dag on main (79f7ffb) and found something worth flagging before the MoE step, since it bears on the Step 4 "verifier only checks the proof, does not re-run" assumption in roadmap.md:58.

verify_shard_dag (compose.rs:1355, forward_ops call at 1368) and verify_committed_shard_dag (compose.rs:1516, forward_ops call at 1537) both do let mut ws = Store{...}; forward_ops(&mut ws, ops) on a fresh clone before checking anything -- forward_ops (compose.rs:722) is the real forward pass: real matmuls via mm_par_fixed, real softmax, real RoPE. Both verify entry points re-run the whole model. That matches the benchmarked numbers -- verify at ~52-70% of prove time tracks a cheaper-but-still-real forward pass, not O(log n) succinct verification. README.md:33 says "verifying it is cheap and does not re-run the model" -- today's wiring does the opposite, including on the committed/WHIR path, not just the plain one.

Concrete cost: the three use cases in the README's own pitch (trustless escrow, on-chain settlement, on-chain governance) all need a verifier that's cheap enough to run in a contract/light client -- none of them can re-run an LLM forward pass. And Step 4's MoE routing design ("not an architectural breakthrough... verifier does not re-run") is built on the same assumption, so it's worth confirming this before investing in V2-Lite.

Separate, smaller one in the new primitive itself: rope.rs's rounding (prove_rope/verify_rope, lines ~146-166) proves the algebraic identity x_f*cos - x_s*sin - 2^shift*out_f - rem_f + half = 0 via a plain sumcheck, but rem_f/rem_s are never range-checked -- no logUp lookup like projection.rs has for its own rounding remainder (projection.rs:3 explicitly calls out "range check as a logUp lookup"). @JimmyShi22 the weights-commitment proposal with real numbers is up: https://github.com/trustless-ai/zkIE/pull/15 (docs and tools only, nothing in the prover changes).

Headline, all measured on e897cca. One WHIR opening of a single weight tensor is 115 KB at 2^22 (129 KB at 2^24), and the verifier runs about 1.9k Poseidon2-16 permutations. I ported your exact Poseidon2 instance to Solidity (bit-exact against Rust on three permutation vectors, the sponge hash and the compression): 52,271 gas per permutation, so about 99.9 M gas of Merkle hashing for one 2^22 opening. A Poseidon2 weights opening is not viable on-chain. The same query and hash counts with a Keccak Merkle tree: 177 k gas of hashing measured, roughly 3 to 5 M gas per opening end to end (estimate, +/- 30%).

The measurements also turned up that Whir::new(n) cannot be built for n >= 26 (PowBitsExceedBudget: required 17 at n=26, 25 at n=27), so a global weights commitment or a 2^26 lm_head needs a bigger PoW budget or commitments of n <= 25.

Three questions are on the PR: a Keccak instance for static weights only, the PoW budget policy, and one commitment per shard or fewer. I'll build whichever you pick.

text_original:
Thanks a lot for this detailed benchmarking and analysis! It’s super clear and very helpful.

Your tests perfectly validate the current on-chain situation: native Poseidon2 Merkle opening is way too gas-heavy for on-chain usage, and Keccak Merkle becomes the only feasible baseline solution for now. We also clearly see the PoW budget limitation for larger tensor sizes starting from n=26.

That said, we think there is still significant room for further optimization beyond per-element Merkle proofs.

We’d suggest you also evaluate cryptographic accumulators, including both RSA accumulators and pairing-based accumulators.

Especially pairing-based accumulators are theoretically more aligned and compatible with the algebraic nature of the existing WHIR framework.

The core advantage is batch membership proof:
Instead of generating and verifying many individual Merkle proofs for every accessed (index, weight) pair, accumulators can verify the entire subset relationship in a single aggregated proof.

This can drastically reduce on-chain verification cost, especially when we open a large number of weight points in one WHIR reduction.

So Merkle trees are a solid baseline, but accumulators are a promising direction to explore for better on-chain efficiency. 🤝

Correctness issue at e897cca — rsqrt coarse step

Jimmy — we hit something at e897cca while staging the Deucalion run. It's a correctness issue rather than a performance one, so flagging it straight away.

bench_sharded on full GPT-2 512 reports argmax 0/512. benchmarks.md (:226, :298) documents 511/512. The proof completes and verifies — it just verifies the wrong computation.

It traces to one character in rsqrt_index (crates/zkie-ops/src/compose.rs:704). Four places specify the coarse quantization step, and three of them agree with each other:


source                                 step
-------------------------------------  ----
doc comment, compose.rs:697            2^8
extract_rsqrt_piecewise.py:20          2^8
  (COARSE_STEP = 1 << 8)
unit test rsqrt_index_piecewise        2^8
implementation, compose.rs:704  >> 16  2^16


The unit test is red at this ref:


test compose::tests::rsqrt_index_piecewise ... FAILED
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: 1048576
 right: 1048577


The fix is the shift:


-        (FINE + ((raw - FINE) >> 16)) as u32
+        (FINE + ((raw - FINE) >> 8)) as u32


With that applied the test passes, the full zkie-ops lib suite is 26/26 green, and GPT-2 512 goes to 511/512 — matching your documented "1 near-tie, fixed-point" exactly. Measured on a 5950X at 32 threads, nothing else changed:


              argmax    prove     verify    peak RSS
e897cca       0/512     95.76 s   68.56 s   33.83 GB
+ fix         511/512   93.46 s   63.49 s   40.90 GB


One detail worth having: the correct path uses more memory, not less (40.9 vs 33.8 GB). The bad index was short-circuiting real work, so any memory figure taken from the current build understates the real requirement.

And the part we did not expect

Against a 16-core desktop (5950X) running the identical patched build:


                  5950X 16c   Deucalion 128c
13-shard prove      90.48 s      68.72 s   1.32x faster
13-shard verify     67.93 s      43.52 s   1.56x faster
1-shard prove      176.81 s     311.38 s   1.76x SLOWER
1-shard verify     159.24 s     203.64 s   1.28x SLOWER


The sharded path gains from more cores. The whole-model path actively degrades. Overall the 128-core node finished 1.27x slower than the desktop (627 s vs 495 s of compute), because the 1-shard phase dominates the wall time.

Two confounds we are not papering over:

• the EPYC's per-core clock is roughly 1.4x lower than the desktop's, and the whole-model path barely parallelises (1.08x from 8 to 32 threads on the desktop), so it is exactly the path most exposed to clock
• this is a single repeat, against three on the desktop where run-to-run spread was 5.8–7.9%

So "more cores hurt" and "this CPU is slower per core" are not yet separated.

A 16 / 32 / 64 / 128 sweep, 3 repeats, is running now on one Deucalion node — same machine throughout, so clock drops out. If 1-shard prove degrades as threads rise on a single machine, that isolates the core-count effect. 8 NUMA domains across 2 sockets is the first suspect.

Will report either way. If it holds, the practical read is that the whole-model path is where parallelism is being lost, and granularity rather than core count is the lever — which would make the autotuner's granularity search the thing that matters, and make big-core-count allocations much less useful for this workload than they look.

Jimmy, the accumulator study is in PR #15 (docs/onchain-accumulators.md, measured gas in test/AccumulatorCost.t.sol, commit e54d4a2). Short version:

- Membership is only the small part of the opening. In our n=22 Keccak estimate, hashing is ~0.18M of ~3-5M; the rest is folding arithmetic (~1.3M) and calldata (1.3-3.2M, half of it path digests). So a free batch-membership check saves at most ~15-40%.
- RSA accumulator: measured modexp costs (2048-bit, 128-bit-exp PoE check 43k; Miller-Rabin round 344). Estimate ~0.7M if the accumulated elements are the 80 opened leaves, ~18M if individual weights. Net gas about a wash, plus a trusted RSA modulus and ~112-bit security. We would not build it.
- Pairing/KZG: measured 113k for a 2-pair opening check, so a batched weights claim is ~0.3-0.4M, constant in model size. That is the cheap path, but it has a field problem: WHIR runs over Goldilocks (and its extension) while a pairing commitment lives over BN254 Fr, so it cannot discharge eval(weights, r) = y at a Goldilocks-extension r.

So the question that decides it: where does zkIE want to go - (a) a field-bridging argument, (b) a weight claim over Fr, or (c) a Groth16/Plonk wrapper with the Poseidon2 weights root as a public input (~0.25-0.3M on-chain for any model size)? Until that is chosen, the Keccak weights-only instance stays the shippable baseline. One cheap, certain gain meanwhile: a Merkle multi-proof (~30% fewer path bytes, estimate).

Jimmy — we hit something at e897cca while staging the Deucalion run. It's a correctness issue rather than a performance one, so flagging it straight away.

bench_sharded on full GPT-2 512 reports argmax 0/512. benchmarks.md (:226, :298) documents 511/512. The proof completes and verifies — it just verifies the wrong computation.

It traces to one character in rsqrt_index (crates/zkie-ops/src/compose.rs:704). Four places specify the coarse quantization step, and three of them agree with each other:


source                                 step
-------------------------------------  ----
doc comment, compose.rs:697            2^8
extract_rsqrt_piecewise.py:20          2^8
  (COARSE_STEP = 1 << 8)
unit test rsqrt_index_piecewise        2^8
implementation, compose.rs:704  >> 16  2^16

test compose::tests::rsqrt_index_piecewise ... FAILED
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: 1048576
 right: 1048577

-        (FINE + ((raw - FINE) >> 16)) as u32
+        (FINE + ((raw - FINE) >> 8)) as u32

@Tmerlini_bot Thanks for the careful framing on the boundary commitment — I agree completely that none of us should just guess at whether a scheme preserves soundness. That's exactly why I want to propose an alternative that avoids the question entirely.

Instead of splitting forward_ops across nodes and passing boundary tensors over the wire, each node can compute its own witness independently:

• Node B runs the forward pass up to its own shard's layer, keeping only that layer's intermediate tensors (its shard's witness) plus the upstream input boundary; everything before is streamed and released as it goes.

• Each node then proves its own shard against the tensors it computed itself — not against anything received from a neighbor.

• The boundary check between nodes is just a consistency safety net (same model, same weights, same input), not the load-bearing part.

The key point is that this removes the trust assumption altogether: node B's witness doesn't depend on a value node A sent it, so there is nothing for A to lie about. And the soundness anchor is unchanged — the verifier still recomputes the full forward pass and checks every shard's claims against the true values, exactly as in the single-node path. So no new cryptographic assumption, no new soundness argument to certify.

The honest cost: each node redundantly runs the (cheap) forward up to its layer — roughly a conical ~20x single-machine inference across all nodes — and each node touches all the weights (mmap'd from Lustre, so I/O not resident memory). Since inference is small relative to proving, we judge this acceptable, and it's structurally simpler than splitting forward + committed hand-offs.

Would love your take on whether this fits your side better than the boundary-commitment route. If it does, we can move straight to building it.

Checked your #11 against the spec text rather than from memory, and there is nothing to correct. A committed policyRoot, the verifier contract, an expiry and a single-use nullifier is right, and so is pre-execution binding to an action commitment and a permitted executor. Gary's privacy framing is right too, the Scope of the privacy claim section says in those words that 8354 hides the policy and not the action.

Two things I would add rather than change. The nullifier is domain-scoped, not only single-use. It is derived in-circuit as H(domainId, agentId, actionCommitment, actionNonce) and isConsumed is keyed on (domainId, nullifier). That bears on the composition question, because a verdict cannot be replayed into a second domain, so it does not travel as standing evidence without re-proving.

The other one is bigger. The rule chugarchugarr landed on in #15, that evidence only authorises the conclusion it establishes, is already written into 8354's own Security Considerations as action-level integrity versus interpreter-level fidelity. A verdict proves the interpreter committed at programKey ran over this action and returned ALLOW. It does not prove that interpreter implements the policy the domain intends, and the spec says plainly that the two look identical on-chain. So a KYA scheme consuming an 8354 verdict gets the first and not the second, and fidelity has to be established out of band. That is a fourth independent arrival at the same rule, which is the part worth saying out loud.

Happy for you to post both, or I will. Say which.

Read #59 at e78eb1d on a cold clone. All four pins recompute, 11/11 vectors reproduce, 8/8 mutants KILLED with 0 survived, 0 crashed and controls preserved. c6 plus M8 do close Pavlo's signature-guard gap, so the mechanics are good.

One real finding before it lands, and it sits in the grade rather than the pins. subject_bound() never looks at the signature. c6 is c2 with one signature byte flipped, and the bodies, corpora and decisions are byte-identical, so subject_bound() returns the same ('NO_FINDING', 'AUTHENTICATED_REPORT') for both. I ran it rather than read it: sig_ok is False on c6 and the grade still comes back AUTHENTICATED_REPORT, while README line 22 defines that grade as the checker having verified an authenticated, manifest-carried assertion. The suite is honest in replay_bindings, but anything reading evidence_grade on its own admits an unsigned report as authenticated.

It is also not pinned in either direction. c6's expect names only replay_failures, and that branch in evaluate() returns on f == expect[replay_failures] alone, so the grade is never asserted on that path. The variance is resolved — it is page cache. Peak RSS is the wrong metric, and it has been UNDERSTATING forward_shard

I said the cause was open and named THP and glibc arenas as the suspects. Both are wrong, and I would rather say so before anyone spends time on them.

Instrumented the benchmark to split RSS into anonymous and file-backed, then ran it 24 times across 4 nodes with arena / trim / mmap tunables varied (job 1979939, seq=16):

                 peak RSS         RssAnon         RssFile
  24 runs     22.7-50.3 GiB   2.59-6.05 GiB    1.7-42.3 GiB
  within grp      ~20 spread     0.00 spread      ~40 spread

RssAnon was constant to two decimals within each group. The entire 27.7 GiB swing is mmap-backed weight pages moving in and out of residency. Since #17 the weights are mmap-backed, and file-backed pages are reclaimable under pressure, so a node does not have to find room for them the way it does for anonymous memory.

Both suspects: THP is not involved — AnonHugePages is 0 in all 24 runs although the nodes have THP set to always. Arenas are not the variance but are a separate real win: arena_max did nothing, trim_threshold=128k cut RssAnon 57% while peak RSS did not move. Measured by peak, a genuine improvement reads as no effect.

=== seq=512, two nodes (job 1979955) ===

  node     config            peak      anon      file
  cnx147   default/full     216.0    205.00       9.0 GiB
  cnx148   default/full     201.6    199.61       0.0
  cnx147   default/shard    106.1     54.73      49.3
  cnx148   default/shard    101.3     54.73       1.8
  cnx147   trim128k/full    163.1    161.06       0.0
  cnx148   trim128k/full    216.8    205.53       9.3
  cnx147   trim128k/shard    93.5     17.58      73.9
  cnx148   trim128k/shard    93.5     17.58      73.9

Two things, and the second qualifies my own recommendation.

1. forward_shard saves much more than we told you. By the metric we published, 223.2 -> 98.0 GiB, 56%. By anonymous memory, 205.0 -> 54.73 GiB, 73% — and 91% with eager trim. We undersold our own change because peak RSS is dominated by page cache. Eager trim takes the shard from 54.73 to 17.58 GiB, a 68% cut at seq=512 against 57% at seq=16, for one environment variable.

2. But RssAnon is NOT universally reproducible, so "just use RssAnon" is too strong. For the SHARDED path it is exact: 54.73/54.73 and 17.58/17.58 across two nodes, spread 0.00, twice. For the whole-graph path it varies — 205.00 vs 199.61, and with trim 205.53 vs 161.06, a 44 GiB spread. I would have claimed reproducibility from the seq=16 runs alone and been wrong a fourth time.

Honest version: RssAnon is the right metric and is exactly reproducible for the path we care about, one shard per node. The whole-graph path is unstable in anonymous memory too, for reasons I have not chased, and it is the path we are replacing anyway.

One consequence to flag rather than claim: 17.58 GiB is below the 29 GiB of an A64FX ARM node — the largest, least contended partition here at 1612 nodes, which we had written off at 98 GiB. I am NOT saying a shard fits one. The weights are a 100 GB mmap and 29 GiB leaves very little room for file residency, so it would likely thrash even though the anonymous requirement fits. It moves ARM from ruled out to worth measuring.

Method note: this thread has had four hypotheses from me about one number today — node memory size, the benchmarks disagreeing, THP, now page cache. Each time I reasoned from a mechanism instead of instrumenting. The anon/file split took ten minutes and should have been first, not fourth. Earlier posts stand except where corrected here.

Instrumentation on PR #26. Logs: rss-variance-1979939.out, anon-512-1979955.out.

  roadmap.md:58  "the verifier only checks the proof (does not re-run)"

here is a proposed Guarantee Preservation Rule based on the two concrete cases. The key distinction is between checking declared dependencies and establishing that those dependencies are sufficient.

Guarantee Preservation Rule — discussion draft v0.1

A downstream consumer MUST NOT claim an inherited guarantee unless:
- The guarantee, subject, scope, assumptions and contract version are identified
- The dependency set has a documented sufficiency justification accepted under the consumer’s policy
- The required predicates and preservation relations are established at the composition boundary
- The downstream claim stays within the established scope and evidence strength

Checking a weaker projection is insufficient. Winner identity alone does not establish payment-policy preservation; an adjacent signature failure flag does not establish that the evidence grade respects authentication.

Proposed shared format

- contract_id / version: profile identity and semantics
- guarantee: the exact claim being evaluated
- subject / scope: bound artifacts, applicability and evaluation context
- authority: applicable evidence authorities and consumer acceptance policy
- depends_on: required predicates, evidence and verification procedures
- dependency_basis: the specification, theorem assumptions or reviewed argument supporting the sufficiency of those dependencies
- establishes / does_not_establish: positive and excluded claims
- evaluation: evaluator version, evidence references, per-dependency outcomes, result and reason codes

The dependency list is itself a claim. Checking every listed predicate cannot establish that no necessary dependency was omitted. A digest binds the supporting argument; it does not prove that argument sound.

Results

PRESERVED: the required relation is established for this subject and scope under the stated assumptions
VIOLATED: admissible evidence demonstrates that a required relation is false
UNVERIFIABLE: evidence, applicability or dependency justification is insufficient to decide

A consumer requiring the guarantee MUST withhold it for both VIOLATED and UNVERIFIABLE. Existing profile verdicts remain visible; mappings into these proposed results must be explicit.

Case A — authentication → evidence grade

In recompute-kit #59, c6 exposed an invalid signature while subject_bound() still produced AUTHENTICATED_REPORT. The fix at a725f2e gates that path on signature validity, pins CANNOT_ESTABLISH/null in c6, and adds M9 for the missing guard.

The proposed format would declare authentication as a dependency of the grade and retain the native verdict. Successful authentication still does not establish scanner-origin execution.
https://github.com/trustless-ai/recompute-kit/pull/59

Case B — award → actual settlement

PRF #13 checks a bounded award-to-settlement relation including actual payment. With cost 60, competing bid 50 and fixed reward 100, truthful bidding gives utility 0; bidding 49 gives +40 under fixed reward versus −10 under Vickrey payment.

The proposed format would make payment-policy preservation explicit. The current profile checks supplied synthetic records; it does not establish chain provenance or universal mechanism truthfulness.
https://github.com/pipavlo82/protected-relation-fixtures/pull/13

Conformance requirement

Each critical dependency should have a positive control, an adverse witness and a mutation control. Assertions must cover the downstream claim itself. These tests expose specific omissions; they do not prove dependency completeness.

Suggested next step

Express both cases in this shared format and compare independent consumer results. Before proposing an ERC, identify the concrete Ethereum producer/consumer interface and its evidence binding, encoding and versioning requirements. That would give the proposal a specific interoperability purpose.

I think the common principle is mature enough to write down explicitly now.
Guarantee Preservation Rule — discussion draft v0.1
A downstream consumer MUST NOT claim that an upstream guarantee is preserved unless:
the exact guarantee, subject, scope, assumptions, authority semantics and contract version are identified;
the relations the guarantee depends on are explicitly declared;
there is a documented basis for why those declared dependencies are sufficient for the guarantee;
the consumer explicitly checks and preserves those relations at the composition boundary;
the downstream claim does not exceed the established scope or evidence strength.
Checking adjacent, weaker, or merely correlated fields is insufficient.
The dependency declaration is itself a claim. Verifying every listed dependency does not prove that no necessary dependency was omitted. A digest can bind the supporting specification, theorem assumptions, or reviewed argument, but cannot establish that the argument is sound.
A possible machine-readable contract could include:
contract_id
version
guarantee
subject
scope
assumptions
authority
depends_on
dependency_basis
establishes
does_not_establish
consumer_checks
evidence_refs
dependency_outcomes
result
reason
The preservation result should remain fail-closed:
PRESERVED — all required preservation relations are established under the declared dependency basis for the bound subject and scope.
VIOLATED — at least one required preservation relation is established false.
UNVERIFIABLE — no required relation is established false, but one or more required relations, applicability conditions, or dependency-basis requirements cannot be established.
A consumer that requires the guarantee MUST withhold that guarantee for both VIOLATED and UNVERIFIABLE.
The same rule is now independently visible in two different domains:
recompute-kit #59 — authentication → evidence grade
An invalid signature could still flow through subject_bound() into AUTHENTICATED_REPORT. The repair makes signature validity load-bearing on that path, pins the downstream grade in the adverse case, and adds a mutation control for removal of the guard.
This shows that observing a signature failure elsewhere is not equivalent to proving that the downstream evidence grade actually depends on authentication.
PRF #13 — award → actual settlement
The upstream Vickrey mechanism can remain correct while a downstream fixed-reward settlement changes the payment relation required by the truthfulness guarantee.
Winner identity is therefore insufficient. The settlement must preserve the theorem-relevant payment relation before the truthfulness guarantee can be inherited.
For conformance, each machine-testable dependency claimed as necessary for preservation should have:
a positive control;
a concrete adverse witness;
a mutation control demonstrating that removing or weakening the dependency check changes the downstream result.
These controls show that a declared boundary is load-bearing. They do not prove that the dependency set is complete.
The next useful step would be to express both existing cases in one neutral guarantee-preservation-v0 schema without changing their native verdicts, then test whether an independent consumer can evaluate both through the same interface.
If that works, there may be a concrete ERC here: a narrow Ethereum interoperability standard for declaring what a guarantee depends on and determining whether a downstream composition is entitled to inherit it, rather than attempting to standardize all of Semantic ABI at once.

Look at what each mode proves about the implementation:

one-core-hour job, not a cluster job. I would rather say that than dress a bit-identical
recomputation up as a big independent result.
Mode 2, fresh stream. Different bytes by design, so there is nothing to compare byte-wise.
Only statistics.
So neither compares bytes across platforms — and that is the check that would catch a
platform-dependent implementation bug: word size, endianness, shift or rotate semantics, anything
undefined that happens to behave on your machine. Which brings the third mode:

Mode 3, fixed-seed determinism. If the build can take a fixed seed and bypass os.urandom

then the same seed must produce the same bytes on any correct implementation. Same seed, two
architectures, compare digests. A mismatch is a real bug in the implementation; a match is the
first claim in your list — code identity — actually established rather than assumed. It is
also cheap: one short stream, not 2 GiB.

  trim128k   mean 196.98 GiB   range 184.82-205.37   spread 20.55  (10.4%)

So the number was roughly double what the data supports. I would rather restate it than leave the inflated one standing.

One detail that narrows it: the variation is run-to-run, not node-to-node. cnx487 alone gave 192.76 and 203.14 on two reps of the same config. So it is not node state.

=== the finding worth more than the question ===

Item 4 was meant to close a loose end. It explains something instead.

  whole-graph path:  default 198.98 -> trim 196.98 GiB  = +1.0%
  one shard:         default  54.73 -> trim  17.58 GiB  = +68%

glibc trim does essentially nothing on the whole-graph path and cuts a shard by more than two thirds. The mechanism is clean: malloc trim can only return memory that was freed, and the whole-graph path frees nothing — every intermediate stays live by construction. forward_shard releases as it goes, which is what gives trim something to return.

So the tunable is not a general win that happens to help us. It is a win BECAUSE of the decomposition, and it would not exist without it. That is a better argument for forward_shard than the raw memory number, because it is causal rather than correlational.

Which also means: anyone benchmarking the whole-graph path and finding trim useless has not found a counterexample to our figure. They have found the absence of the thing that makes it work.

You are right, and the arithmetic says so clearly enough that I should have done it before making the claim.

The r=4 logistic map has Lyapunov exponent lambda = ln 2, so the amplification per iteration is almost exactly a factor of 2 — one bit per iteration. Over 20 iterations that is 2^20:

  1 ulp relative in double  = 2^-52
  after 20 iterations       = 2^-52 x 2^20 = 2^-32

So the two values still agree to about 32 bits of mantissa, roughly 10 significant decimal digits. Not decorrelated, not close to it. Full mantissa divergence needs around 52 iterations and the implementation does 20. My "within a few hundred iterations the streams are unrelated" was describing a map that runs long enough to do it, and yours does not.

So measuring the first divergence point is the right call and I would add one thing to it: whether the OUTPUT diverges is then governed by the extractor, not by the chaos. A 2^-32 relative difference lives in the low ~20 mantissa bits. An extractor consuming low-order bits sees that immediately; one consuming high-order bits may see nothing at all. So output divergence is still likely, but if it happens the mechanism would be extractor bit-selection rather than chaotic decorrelation — and those want distinguishing in the record, because they imply different things about portability.

Which makes the shape of your divergence curve more informative than the first point alone:

  divergence at iteration 1-2        direct propagation, chaos is irrelevant
  divergence growing ~1 bit per iter chaos contributing exactly as lambda = ln 2 predicts
  no divergence at 20                the FP path is bit-identical, 3A and 3B both pass

The third outcome is the one worth hoping for and it is not implausible — 20 iterations is short, and if NumPy dispatches the same kernels on both machines the inputs may be identical to begin with. Worth recording which bits the extractor consumes alongside the divergence point, so the two mechanisms can be told apart afterwards rather than argued about.

And accepted on FMA: written as NumPy array operations, each ufunc materialises its own rounded intermediate, so there is no multiply-add for a compiler to contract across. My hypothesis applies to scalar compiled code, not to array expressions. Your framing — testable rather than assumed, with build metadata pinned either way — is the right one, and the fingerprint you have added covers it.

Correcting my own post, and I have the root cause.

First, the correction, which is embarrassing in a useful way. I told this thread that a
conformance check has to enumerate rather than sample a default page. My own numbers were sampled.
I read `/records?limit=5000` and reported 302 / 483 / 419. The endpoint silently caps at 500 per
page and returns a `cursor` — it does not error, it does not warn, it just gives you 500 and a
pointer you have to notice. And there is a second namespace, `agent-attestations:wyriwe`, that the
default view does not show at all.

Enumerated properly, paginating the cursor and asking both namespaces:

                    agent-attestations    agent-attestations:wyriwe
  NAS (0.7.0)              302                      299
  Railway (0.8.0)          483                     1725
  ENSBoiler (origin)       419                      413

So the divergence is roughly six times worse than I reported in the namespace that matters, and I
understated it by doing precisely the thing I was warning about. The `limit` parameter being
silently clamped rather than rejected is the trap — a checker asking for 5000 and receiving 500 has
no signal that it got a page instead of the set.

Second correction: I listed ENSBoiler as "missing" records. That was wrong framing. It is an Origin;
it holds what it produces and does not pull from routers. Its counts are correct by design.

Now the root cause, and it is directly a 8309 matter.

The NAS node runs 0.7.0. Railway runs 0.8.0. The divergence-preservation work landed in
between — `1caf220` "preserve multi-vantage divergence in the mesh store", `e1ba6fd` "signature-keyed
attestation retention", `aae4a34` "canonicalize signatures (low-s) before the dedup key", `3ce2a76`
"test the double-sign detector".

0.7.0 keys retention by `inputHash`. So when the same input legitimately has successive or
multi-vantage attestations — same `inputHash`, different `value`, different `timestamp`, different
signature — 0.7.0 does not read that as divergence to preserve. It reads it as equivocation. The
node's log is a wall of:

[double-sign] input_hash=0x6ba8a383… ns=agent-attestations:wyriwe
              signer=https://gateway.ensub.org — flagged for future slashing

That is our own origin being flagged for slashing, repeatedly, for behaving correctly. The records
arrive — one sync pass logged `+2208 inserted, 0 rejected` — and the node keeps 299 of them.

So the mesh did not drift because sync was broken. It drifted because one node was running code from
before the retention rule existed, and that code silently discards exactly what the rule was written
to preserve. Signature-keyed retention is not a refinement; without it a node quietly converges to a
single value per input and calls everything else a double-sign.

Two things I think this says for the spec:

1. The retention key belongs in the normative text, not just the implementation. If 8309 does not
   state that attestations are retained keyed by signature (post-canonicalization), an implementer
   reading the spec can write 0.7.0's behaviour and believe they are conformant. We did.
2. A double-sign finding needs a conformance case that distinguishes equivocation from divergence.
   Ours cannot currently tell them apart, and the failure mode is silent and punitive — it flags an
   honest peer for slashing. A detector that cannot produce a known-good "this is divergence, not
   equivocation" result is a detector whose positives are unbacked.

On our side the remediation is in flight rather than done: the NAS is being moved to 0.8.0 so it
carries the retention work (DB backed up first, since the identity key changes). I will post the
enumerated counts again once it is up, pass or fail — if signature-keyed retention does not close
the gap, that is more interesting than if it does and I would rather this thread saw it either way.

Happy to write both up as PR text against 8309 if that is useful.

text_original: Thanks, Echo. The enumerated counts and the inputHash-keyed retention root cause are the useful part; the signature-keyed retention point is worth keeping in the spec text. We'll read the 0.8.0 re-check when it lands.

The NAS now runs 0.8.0. Origin records are fully replicated on both routers:

                     origin holds    NAS      Railway
  agent-attestations      419       419/419   419/419

Where I was wrong. I set the check to watch NAS :wyriwe climb toward Railway's 1725 and it

own locally-originated records, present on no other node — 0 on the NAS, 0 on the origin. I had
picked a convergence target that included records which were never going to replicate from it. The
honest version is that "is the mesh converged" is not answerable by comparing totals at all; it is
only answerable per-origin, asking whether every node holds what each origin produced.

That is probably the more useful thing for 8309 than my earlier two points. A convergence
predicate over node totals is not well-formed. Totals include locally-originated records, so two
correct nodes can legitimately differ, and two broken ones can accidentally match. The predicate has
to be: for each origin O and namespace N, every participating node holds the complete set O
produced in N. That is checkable, it is what we actually verified above, and it does not depend on
nodes being identical.

One new question I cannot answer, flagging rather than sitting on it. Those 1312 records are
locally-originated on a node whose declared type is Router. Our own taxonomy says Routers relay and
Origins produce. Either the taxonomy is wrong about what a Router does, our node is mislabelled, or
it is originating records it should not. I do not know which yet, and it is the kind of thing the
node-type field was supposed to make legible — which connects back to nodeType not being inside the
signed envelope, since a node's declared role is currently an unverifiable assertion about itself.

Still happy to write the retention-key and equivocation-vs-divergence points up as PR text.

text_original:
Echo, the per-origin predicate is the right result: totals can't answer "converged", and you showed why with your own numbers.

A split that keeps each point where it belongs:

- Base 8309 (your PR): retention keyed by signature, not inputHash, so legitimate multi-vantage re-attestations are kept as divergence, not discarded as equivocation.
- The 8309-vantage companion (we'll take it): the conformance rules.
  1. Convergence is checked per origin and per namespace: every node holds the complete set each origin produced. Node totals are not a valid predicate.
  2. Sync checks enumerate through the cursor. A clamped or default page is a sample, and a sample can't pass a conformance check.
  3. Every field a peer acts on, nodeType included, is inside the signed envelope. A declared role outside it is an unverifiable claim.

Each rule ships with test vectors (the paginated-cursor trap, double-sign vs divergence, nodeType outside the envelope) in our conformance repo, credited to your findings. I'll post the PR here when it's up.

Latest on the verify cost — the useful part is that most of the gap was a fixable bug, and the numbers now point clearly at what to do next. All measured on GPT-2 512, 13 shards (`docs/batch-opening-2026-10-07.md`, `docs/reedweave-assessment-2026-10-07.md`).

1. A pre-existing parallelism bug in committed verify — fixed, ~8.3×. verify_committed_shard_dag was looping shards serially and calling verify_shard, which clones the full witness store and re-runs forward_ops per shard — 13 shards meant ~13 full-store clones plus ~13 forward passes, on top of the single forward the cross-bind step already does. That serial loop is on main: it came in with the committed shard DAG (2026-09-30), and the 2026-10-01 parallel-verify change fixed the plain verify_shard_dag but missed the committed one. It now mirrors the plain path — one forward_ops, then parallel verify_shard_precomputed. Committed verify: 184 s → 22 s (~8.3×).

2. Multi-point / batch opening. One commitment plus one batched opening proof covering several points, instead of a commitment/proof per point; the boundary tensors use it for cross-shard binding — one shared boundary commitment, no second commitment and no linking proof. Measured after the fix: WHIR open + verify is ~0.56 s of the 22 s (~2.5 %) — open_stats 0.53 s + verify_stats 0.03 s over 70 openings.

3. Succinctness is a real, open problem right now. After the fix, ~20 s of the 22 s verify is the single forward-pass recompute — the verifier still has to re-derive the witness instead of just checking openings, so verification is not succinct yet. This is the Layer-1 gap, it is the largest single item in the verify budget, and it is what we are working through now (tracked in #15). The lever is a claim-driven verifier: open the boundary/weight/I-O anchors instead of recomputing the forward. It is a ~20× class of change, not a sub-second one.

https://github.com/trustless-ai/zkIE/pull/29

The contract anchors sha256(raw) without checking canonical form. The statement goes in as calldata, so the bytes are public. Anyone can prove non-canonical form within a window using Zexo's isCanonical, and the full check only runs on dispute.

ML-DSA-65 binding, 4120 B: 106k vs 1,065k checked on chain, about 10x

The optimistic path is roughly flat in size because one storage write dominates. A challenger pays 15k to 982k depending on where the first violation is, so the bond has to cover the worst case.

Answering as 8373 author, and the measurements deserve saying first: 10x on the ML-DSA-65 binding, the trust assumption named rather than buried, and seven tests where removing each guard reds exactly one of them. Using Zexo's checker and vectors unchanged is also the right call — a second canonicality implementation would have made any disagreement ambiguous.

On the spec question: no, the statement should keep the key itself. And I do not think you need the change.

The spec enforces under the key, not merely about it. §84: "Enforcement keys only on anchored times, the content-address, and pq_pubkey". §115: "verify the PQ companion over the artifact's content-address under the in-force pq_pubkey". The resolver returns resolved_pq_pubkey, and the admit test is literally binds_key = c["pq_pubkey"] == resolved["pq_pubkey"].

So a hash-only statement is not a smaller statement — it is a different trust model. An enforcer holding only H(key) cannot verify the companion at all; it has to fetch the key out of band, and then correctness depends on that fetch succeeding. We would be trading a bounded gas cost for an unbounded availability assumption, on the one field the verdict is computed under.

And your construction already gets the cap without touching the spec. You wrote it yourself: "The statement goes in as calldata, so the bytes are public." That is the answer — the statement stays whole and self-verifiable, availability is satisfied by calldata, and the chain stores 32 bytes. The size cap you want is achieved at the anchoring layer. Moving it into the statement layer would remove the key from the thing whose purpose is to bind it.

One place the key hash would not have helped anyway. The worst-case challenge still scales with statement size, and capping the key does not cap the statement — isCanonical runs over the whole JCS document, not the key field. Other members remain unbounded. So the bond would still have to cover a worst case you cannot derive from the key type.

The lever for that looks like it is in your layer, not ours. You already observed the challenger pays 15k–982k depending on where the first violation is. That dependence is the opening: if the challenger supplies the index of the first non-canonical byte and the contract verifies canonicality locally at that offset rather than re-running the full pass, the challenge cost goes roughly flat and the bond becomes derivable instead of worst-case. That is the usual fraud-proof move — pinpoint rather than re-execute. Stated as a direction, not a result; I have not implemented it and the local-check predicate is where it would be hard, since JCS violations are not all locally decidable (member ordering and duplicate detection need more than a window).

One practical cost worth putting on the record. The content-address is computed over the statement, so changing what the statement carries changes every content-address. There are already anchored bindings under kya.pq_key_binding.v0, including a rotation at epoch 1. 8373 is Draft so a breaking change is permitted, but it would not be free — it forks the address of everything already anchored, and the migration would need its own answer before the saving is real.

If statement size does become the binding constraint for a future key type, I would rather bound it explicitly in the cutoff profile — a declared maximum, so the bond is computable — than remove the key. That keeps enforcement self-contained and still gives you the derivable worst case.

Separately, @zexoverz: your run on #15 is the more alarming finding of the day and it belongs next to this one. A wrong selector printing PASS through run_conformance while failing through gate.py is the same class of defect as an unchallenged non-canonical statement being accepted — in both cases the check exists and nothing routes the verdict through it.

text_original:
Echo, we built the pinpoint version: https://github.com/babyblueviper1/erc8373-optimistic-jcs/commit/907bc7f

You named the hard part: whether a byte is a violation depends on state the byte doesn't show (inside a string or not, and the previous member name for ordering). So the anchorer commits that state. With the statement, it submits a trace of parser checkpoints at most 256 bytes apart, from INIT to DONE, and only keccak(trace) is stored. A challenger re-runs one segment and wins if it doesn't land exactly on the next checkpoint. If every segment is valid and the trace starts at INIT and ends at DONE, then by induction every checkpoint is the true state, so a non-canonical statement, or a wrong trace, always has one provable bad segment.

On the ML-DSA-65 statement:
challenge, violation at byte 13: 16.8k (was 14.7k)
violation mid-document: 17.5k
violation at the last byte: 116k (was 982k)
anchor: 60.6k + 3.5k trace calldata (was 40.3k)

The worst case is now one segment plus one member-name comparison, whatever the position, so the bond can be computed instead of covering the worst case.

One profile addition makes the ordering rule bounded: member names are capped at 64 escaped bytes. The longest in Zexo's 4693 vectors is 27. On all 4693, at two segment sizes, the trace verdict matches isCanonical exactly. Removing each of 7 guards turns a test red, and 17 tests pass from a cold clone. Zexo's checker is unchanged; the step machine ports its code.

That cap is the declared maximum you suggested putting in the cutoff profile. Would you take a name-length bound plus a max statement size there as the two parameters the bond derives from? If so, we can draft the profile text against these numbers.

source_payload.reply_to_message_text:
Yes to both parameters — but not in the cutoff facet, and the size cap needs care that the name cap does not.

Seventeen minutes from "stated as a direction, not a result" to a measured implementation. And you solved the part I flagged as hard rather than routing around it: committing the parser state so a byte's legality stops depending on context the byte does not show. The induction is what carries it — every segment valid, trace INIT to DONE, therefore every checkpoint is the true state, therefore a non-canonical statement or a wrong trace always has one provable bad segment. That is the guarantee. The 4693-vector agreement is strong corroboration, but it is Zexo's corpus and corpus agreement does not bound adversarial inputs. Separate facet, not /cutoff-enforcement. §84 scopes enforcement to anchored times, the content-address and pq_pubkey, and §229 says v1 over v0 changes exactly two things, both in the cutoff rule — that tightness is deliberate. A name-length bound and a size cap are canonicalization constraints, a different axis. 2. 🔴 The size cap must not become an algorithm fork. This is the one to get right. ML-DSA-65 statements are 4120 B and SLH-DSA 293 B — 14x, driven purely by key size. The ERC already says algorithm is "a field, not a fork: implementations under different NIST families MUST converge on the same content-address rules through canonicalization alone." A cap chosen from today's gas economics could admit one family and exclude another, and size would become a de facto fork against an existing MUST.

So: derive the cap from the largest family the profile admits, state the derivation in the text, and let a larger-key profile raise it. Please do not fix it from the ML-DSA-65 figure alone — otherwise the cheapest family to challenge quietly becomes the only conforming one.

The name cap has none of that problem. 64 escaped bytes against a longest-observed 27 is generous, and it is the bound that makes the ordering rule locally decidable, which was the actual blocker.

3. Enforced at admission, not merely assumed for bond math. If an over-cap statement can still be anchored, it is accepted on-chain and un-challengeable within the derived bond — the bond would be sound only for statements that already complied, which is the wrong direction for a safety property. Both caps need to be rejection rules at admission, with a vector for each.

Per-profile and versioned, never a protocol constant — a future scheme with larger keys should be addable by declaring a new profile, not by amending the ERC.

On that basis, yes: go ahead and draft the profile text. If you put the derivation for the size cap in the PR body rather than only the number, I can review the reasoning rather than just the value.

ids are not rejected anywhere:

select(candidates=[a, a, b], k=2)  ->  winners ['a', 'a']
A duplicated id takes two pool slots, the digest hashes [“a”,“a”,“b”] happily, the commitment

doesn’t give you fair selection unless the consumer preserves the relation — our own consumer has a
path where a malformed candidate set produces a provably unfair draw. It’s a mutant we never wrote,
and you’d have hit it the moment you implemented against the spec rather than against our code.

protocol for the statistical witness, and the archive-identity point stated as a boundary rather than

recoverable from loose files.

Fede's list is right and I'd build it. One addition, from the thing that bit us before.

Every case there is accept-or-reject. A verifier that cannot reach the chain for chainId — wrong network, no RPC, pruned history — falls off the end of that list, and a binary checker has only two things it can do with it, both wrong: accept on the facilitator's word, or reject a proof that may well be sound.

That's the silent-skip shape: the skip path never touches the verdict. So:

• positive → verified
• the five negatives → rejected
• chainId unreachable / receipt not retrievable → unverifiable. Never accepted, never silently passed.

Tri-state, fail-closed, the same way conventions.py verify() resolves an unknown convention hash. Worth a seventh vector with its own mutation control: a verifier that collapses unverifiable into either accepted or rejected must fail it.

Two smaller things while the shape is still open:

1. If this outcome feeds winRate, the proof should carry the governing_convention_hash the score was issued under — win_rate.bps.v0, 0x0501b75d…68daf, live-pinned on /ledger. Recomputing the settlement correctly and then scoring it under a different rounding convention is a seam we've already closed once; worth not reopening it here.

2. The coverage clause from August applies downstream: a feed that publishes the score without settled_count alongside it is non-conformant, because it collapses "not enough history" into "poor outcomes". verifyOutcome is where that history starts being counted.

Credit as Fede has it — Petchevere for the gap, Pavlo for the boundary framing. And none of this pre-empts OnThe_Stars on the semantics; it's additive to that, not ahead of it.

- Recomputed from the receipt only — status, the release event at releaseLogIndex with the orderId topic, payee and amount, and the same-receipt Transfer escrow -> provider. No block scan, no facilitator report. That closes the x402#3824 shape.

One note for the record, non-blocking: this pins a proof format where verifyOutcome was "implementation-defined", so confirm the ERC-8275 spec body and the IAgentReputation NatSpec stay consistent — the NatSpec now names this profile, and the spec body shouldn't leave "implementation-defined" as the only description of what proof is.

Adding an independent audit on top of the approve — we ran the code, not just read it:

Verified by execution:
- python3 check.py → 10/10 vectors reproduced
- python3 check.py --mutants → 9/9 lax checkers caught
- Re-derived both event topics with cast keccak → Released(bytes32,bytes32,bytes32,address,uint256) and Transfer(address,address,uint256) match the pinned literals byte-for-byte
- generate_vectors.py | cmp - verify-outcome-v0.vectors.json → byte-identical

No bypass found: the checker recomputes from the receipt only, and every rule has exactly one vector that tests it.

One design seam worth pinning (chain vs off-chain):

The v0 profile describes an *off-chain* verifier — check.py stands in for eth_getTransactionReceipt and recomputes the settlement. But the on-chain verifyOutcome(bytes32 orderId, bytes calldata proof) external view cannot itself read a historical receipt: a Solidity view function has no eth_getTransactionReceipt, no way to fetch the release event or the Transfer by log index. So the "recompute from the chain alone" guarantee as written lives off-chain. On-chain, verifyOutcome has to accept a *carrier* of that recomputation — a Merkle proof against a published settlement root, a state proof, a signed receipt digest — and verify the carrier, not the receipt.

That is consistent with "other formats remain implementation-defined", but it should be stated explicitly in the spec so "chain-recomputable" isn't misread as "the on-chain function recomputes it". The three states (verified / rejected / unverifiable) are the off-chain checker's; the on-chain bool collapses rejected and unverifiable to false, which is correct, but that mapping deserves to be spelled out.

Two minor notes, neither blocking:
- transfer_ok defaults a missing Transfer data to 0x0, so an order with amount == 0 and a Transfer log missing its data field would pass the amount check. Amounts are never 0 in practice, but pin the field as required for tightness.
- chainId is compared with != (strict), so a proof carrying "8453" (string) against an order carrying 8453 (int) would be rejected. Fine for the fixture; the live adapter should normalize both to one type.

Still approve. Credit stands: Petchevere (gap), Pavlo (boundary framing), Echo (tri-state + coverage).

Pavlo, read #4 at ee1143f and probed the evaluator directly. The full validate needs your prepared node/native toolchain, which we didn't rebuild, so this is predicate-level, not a full replay.

One concrete finding, and it's your own thesis inside your own model: checker independence is not an obligation. O08 (authority) only checks signer == policy.authorized[role] for each role, and nothing in src/v4 compares signers across roles. Set the judgment signer to the provenance (producer) key and have the policy authorize that key for judgment: authority() still returns VERIFIED. So a producer that judges its own output can pass every declared check and C, the same "all declared checks pass while a required obligation is missing" case, with the missing obligation being independence.

Suggested close: an O14 checker_independence (judgment signer != provenance signer, possibly != receipt signer too), required in the output contract, plus a negative self_judged scenario (expect REFUTED) and an omitted_O14 row so the coverage alarm fires when it's dropped. Our work-acceptance records apply the same rule (checker key != producer key, refused before signing if a key can't be compared), so it's a requirement you can check in a real record format, not only in the lab.

Everything else I checked held up: an empty requirement set fails closed (combine([]) is UNVERIFIABLE), unknown contract obligations go UNVERIFIABLE, and counterfeit_definition is caught because the contract pins verification_procedure.

One finding, inside your own trust assumptions. The C result doesn't say what it authorized. evaluate() returns C = {status, authorized}, with no claim_type, scenario or contract hash.

Witness: take negative_O13 (claim.outputHash = 0x55…55, not the real output). Under the output contract it is REFUTED. Now build the same claim the way positive_replay does: replay contract, its scenario and claim_type, catalog filtered to its requirements. It comes back VERIFIED, authorized = true. The claim still carries the false outputHash, and the result doesn't mark it as a field nothing checked.

Every step here is honest under your rules. Replay doesn't consume O13, and contract choice is out of scope, as FORMAL_MODEL §4 says. But anyone downstream who keeps {claim, authorized: true} holds an authorization over a false output claim, with nothing in the result telling them it was replay-only. It's the same shape as the 'absence is not difference' gap from today's x402 thread: a field that is present but never checked reads as if it passed.

Two small fixes would close it:
1. C carries {scenario, claim_type, contract_sha256}, so the authorization names what it was measured against.
2. Claim fields that no selected obligation consumes are either refused or listed (unconsumed_claim_fields), never silently carried.

Our work-acceptance records do the first: the signed receipt carries the sha256 of the criteria it was judged against, so a pass can't be moved to other criteria. If it helps, I can open a PR with the vector (unconsumed-output-under-replay) and both guards, each with a mutation control.

A few technical points worth tightening before merging:
Attention isn't entirely linear. Softmax introduces nonlinearity, so the statement that all nonlinearity lives in the MLP needs correcting.
The Q = K = I example. Softmax doesn't preserve the identity matrix. For a row [1, 0, 0], it produces approximately [0.576, 0.212, 0.212], not [1, 0, 0].
LayerNorm geometry. LayerNorm doesn't generally preserve angles or distances between token representations, since normalization is applied independently to each token.
These are small corrections, but they matter if the notes become a technical reference for zkIE and future verification research.

Thanks for the careful review, Pavlo — these are exactly the kind of technical corrections that matter for a reference doc, really appreciate it.
You're right on all three points:
Softmax nonlinearity — I had it wrong saying attention is "entirely linear." The Q/K/V projections and the final weighted sum of V are linear, but softmax itself introduces nonlinearity; the MLP adds a second nonlinearity via its activation. Updated §03 and §07 to make that distinction clear.
Q = K = I example — you're correct that softmax doesn't preserve the identity matrix. The row [1, 0, 0] maps to roughly [0.576, 0.212, 0.212], not [1, 0, 0]. Fixed the worked example to compute Out₀ ≈ 16.4 instead of the wrong 10.
LayerNorm geometry — the "point cloud" was just a loose intuition, and per-token normalization does change the shape / angles / distances. Updated the wording to describe it as per-token standardization for numeric stability, not a rigid geometric transform.
All three fixes are pushed to the PR (commit 06d9264d). Let me know if anything still looks off, happy to adjust further.🤝

A takeaway from Lisbon Digital Summit today (a Web Summit pre-event) that I'd like the group's read on. It was a broad, sales-oriented event, mostly business people from companies in the area, so a good read of how this lands outside our bubble.

Very few people there were technical, and most companies didn't know that an agent's actions could be recomputed in the user's own browser at all. Only two conversations went properly into it: one at Cisco's stand, and Google Cloud's talk, which felt well aligned with recomputation.

That sparked an idea: most of the companies there would benefit from what /verify does, but not from a pitch that leads with a chain. "Your platform's agents can recompute their actions in your customer's browser" is simpler to sell, and much more accessible.

So the question: what would it take for a non-crypto platform to drop this in? Something like a "Verify" badge next to an agent action that recomputes the receipt in the customer's browser and checks it against a public tamper-evident log, with no chain vocabulary anywhere on screen.

Mapping it against what we already have:
• recompute-lens is most of the end-user side: browser-only, tri-state verdicts, never a bare green, golden-vector self-tests. It's a standalone app today, not an embeddable component.
• receiptos-c14n-v0 (JCS + sha256) is already a receipt profile with no chain in it. @Pavlentyy82, could it be the base for a generic "agent action receipt", or is it too ReceiptOS-specific?
• agent-sdk has the recompute functions, but organised per ERC.
• Missing: an anchor-check recipe (it's on the lens roadmap), and an embeddable build of the lens.

Those three missing pieces feel like commons work: CC0, useful to anyone. On the Vértice side we'd build the hosted plug-in on top (emitter SDK, managed anchoring, packaging for enterprises), the same split as everything else.

Does this fit how you see the lens and the receipt profiles evolving? And is anyone already working on the anchor-check recipe?

Thanks for flagging this — the GPS brute-force result is a real privacy issue, and I agree it should be addressed before the client sandbox.
From the ReceiptOS canonicalization side, I don't see a collision.
A blinding member containing exactly 32 CSPRNG-generated bytes encoded as 64 lowercase hex characters is a normal JSON string. If it lives inside committed content, it participates in canonicalization and hashing.
The historical receiptos-c14n-v0 profile only excludes the top-level anchor when computing receipt_root. It does not strip nested content.blinding.
One distinction worth preserving: DEILS sha256(JCS(content)) and the ReceiptOS receipt root are separate commitment domains. I wouldn't silently treat them as interchangeable.
My preference on the three questions:
1. MUST always for privacy-protected leg-2 content, regardless of estimated entropy. Require fresh, independently generated 256-bit blinding per commitment, with strict encoding validation. Keep it private until authorized disclosure.
2. Selective disclosure: I'd use a separately versioned profile with per-field blinded commitments and a Merkle root, binding field identity and type to each leaf. This avoids changing the existing leg-2 reveal semantics.
3. Negative controls: Definitely. The unblinded GPS dictionary-recovery witness and blinded counterpart would make the privacy boundary testable. I'd also include wrong blinding, reused blinding, altered coordinates and cross-field substitution cases.
Two additional points:
GPS numeric representation must be explicitly defined for cross-runtime JCS compatibility. ReceiptOS's restricted canonical JSON domain does not admit arbitrary floating-point coordinates.
A blinded commitment provides hiding before disclosure, but it does not enforce provider/wallet-only access. That requires separate authenticated encryption and authorization. A public reveal would expose the coordinates to everyone.

gm all. A DEILS leg-2 note from planning a real client sandbox.

We're scoping a sandbox for a location-based client: agents place things at real-world points, and the client wants a receipt for every action with GPS, but readable only by the provider or wallet owner, not the public. That's leg 2 exactly: existence public, content held behind a commitment, revealed on trigger. So the plan is to make the sandbox gateway the first running leg-2 implementation, with a real partner rather than a demo.

While planning it, we found a gap. Leg 2 pins content_commitment = "sha256:" + hex(sha256(JCS(content))) with no salt, and the spec assumes the content is verdict payloads or artifact hashes, which are high-entropy. GPS isn't. We tested it with our reveal checker's own commit(): a commitment to {lat, lon, accuracy}, an attacker who only knows the rough ~1 km block, and a grid search at 1e-5°. The exact coordinates came back in 1.4 s on a Mac mini. The commitment hid nothing.

Proposed fix, with no change to the formula or the reveal state machine: a blinding member inside content (≥256-bit, CSPRNG, fresh per commitment, held with the private content and revealed with it). Control run: with blinding, even the true coordinates don't match without the salt; reveal with salt gives content_bound, wrong salt gives content_commitment_mismatch. Our checker works unchanged.

Questions for the group:
1. MUST always, or MUST only for low-entropy content? (We lean MUST always: it's harmless for high-entropy content and nobody has to judge entropy.)
2. Selective disclosure: the client may want to reveal coordinates without the rest of the receipt. Per-field blinded commitments, or a Merkle root over them (SD-JWT style)? Is that a leg-2 profile or a separate one?
3. We can add a low_entropy_unblinded vector to the neutral set (the brute-force above, which must recover the content) plus its blinded counterpart, which must not. That's a check that can be shown to fail.

@babyblueviper1 since leg 2 / /prove is yours, does a blinding field collide with anything you've planned for the content extension? @Pavlentyy82 any c14n concern with a hex blinding string under receiptos-c14n-v0?

Sandbox only starts once the client sends their exact receipt fields, so there's no rush. We just wanted it in the spec discussion before we build on it.

+1 on the architecture, Pavlo, and on starting small in recompute-lens (now CC0): a browser recipe for the action-subject and anchor-proof profiles first, then the <recompute-lens> component. Those three boundaries are the right ones to keep explicit.

On ReceiptOS joining the org: trustless-ai doesn't belong to anyone, so it isn't mine to grant. Personally it sounds reasonable: it would represent your work inside the commons, and there's precedent, since agent-sdk already lives in the org under Apache-2.0. But it should be a group decision. Options for everyone to weigh in on: (a) move it into the org, (b) keep it independent and list it in the primitives index as an external implementation. @Jimmyshi @babyblueviper1 @zexoverz @DamonZwicker, thoughts?

@Pavlentyy82 @babyblueviper1 Tiago's call on the /prove HOLD is option A: the version is authenticated in the same record as the commitment.

Proposed v1 spec text:
A verifier MUST obtain the profile from the same authenticated record as the commitment (signature or anchor), so that changing either one invalidates the record. A profile stated only in an unauthenticated response, or inside the committed content, is never authority.

It's the same pattern we use for tree heads: we anchor {treeSize, root} together, because a root alone doesn't bind its own interpretation.

The mechanism is Fede's. Whatever /prove already signs or anchors carries profile next to content_commitment. Fede, your plan (version outside the content, in the /prove response) fits this, as long as that response is the signed record.

Integration stays on HOLD until Fede confirms how /prove binds it.

@Pavlentyy82 we ran our own /prove canonicalization against your v1 vectors at ce122d18. That answers the byte-vector question in your PROVE_COMPATIBILITY.md.

It caught a real bug on our side. /prove was hashing Python's sorted JSON, not RFC 8785 JCS, so utf16_key_order and wrong_codepoint_canonicalization came out different (code-point vs UTF-16 key order, and float form like 1e-07 vs 1e-7). Fixed and deployed: /prove commitments and reveals now hash JCS, and all 24 vectors that carry canonical bytes match byte for byte. Every commitment we'd already issued hashes identically under both forms, so none of them changed.

On the rest of your list:
- Blinding: v0 content has none and nothing is added before hashing. A v1 blinding field will live inside content, per the spec.
- Numeric domain: JCS. Content outside it (an integer above 2^53, a non-finite float) still falls back to the old form. We'll make that a refusal before v1.
- Withheld: existence (the commitment and ledger_position) is always public. Content stays held until reveal binds it, and a mismatch is terminal.
